title: Photographers Protest Australia’s Plans to Weaken Copyright Laws for AI
summary: Photographers protest Australian government plans to weaken copyright laws for artificial intelligence
detailed: More than 7,000 photographers, writers, and musicians published a statement protesting the Australian government's proposals to weaken copyright laws for AI companies.
The proposed changes would allow AI companies to train commercial models on copyrighted work without permission or payment as long as it occurs on Australian soil.
Over 7,000 creators, the Australian government, and Isabelle Doran, CEO of the Association of Photographers, are involved.
The protest highlights that unlicensed AI training exploits creators without consent and uses copyright as an economic bargaining chip.
sentences: Photographers have signed a statement protesting the Australian government’s plans to weaken copyright law to benefit AI companies.
According to multiple reports, the Australian government is considering weakening copyright law in order to attract investment from overseas AI companies.
Under the proposals, AI companies would no longer be required to get permission from rights holders before training commercial AI models on their work.
Most of the world’s leading AI companies are known to build their models by using copyrighted work without permission or payment.
The changes proposed by the Australian government would legalize this unlicensed training on copyrighted work, as long as it happened on Australian soil.

Now more than 7,000 photographers, writers, and musicians have come together to publish a statement opposing proposed changes to Australian copyright law that would favor AI companies and weaken copyright law.
“The Australian government must not legalise the theft of the work of the world’s creators on their soil,” the statement reads.
“Creators, such as photographers and image-makers, have little bargaining power against the might of big tech,” Doran says in a statement.
“We have been absolutely clear, creators’ work has been exploited without consent, and any Opt-Outs proposal, which has proven to be burdensome, should not be forced onto creators.
She warns that Australia’s ambitions to become more competitive in the AI sector should not come at the expense of creators’ rights.
“It’s imperative that the Australian Government doesn’t backtrack on its initial commitment to protect creators, both in Australia and across the globe,” Doran explains.

“Copyright is a human right and critically the lifeblood of creators; this basic human right cannot and should not be used as an economic bargaining chip for national AI investment.”
The widespread use of copyrighted material by leading AI companies without permission or compensation has prompted around 150 major lawsuits in the U.S., with rights holders alleging unauthorized use of their work.
